title: Office Headshot Poses That Make a Statement
summary: Headshot poses for professional photos: shoulder angle, chin position, hand placement, and the seated and standing options that read best.
body_markdown:
## Finding that professional pose that gets profile clicks


*Sitting hands your forearms somewhere to land, which is most of the hand problem gone.*


‍


Your headshot gets looked at for about a second and a half, at roughly the size of a postage stamp, on a phone, next to eleven other people's. That is the format. Not a gallery wall.


So almost everything you can control lives in a very small area: shoulder line, chin, jaw, eyes, mouth. The suit matters less than you think. The angle of your shoulders matters enormously, and almost nobody adjusts it.


Bad headshots are rarely badly lit or badly shot. They are usually a person standing square to a camera with their chin tucked and their arms glued to their sides, which is what every human body does by default when a lens points at it. Three adjustments fix most of it.


## Shoulder angle, the one nobody adjusts


*The near shoulder sits a little lower. The shoulder drop signals less tension and a more relaxed demeanor.*


Standing square makes you as wide as you will ever be and removes every line from the frame. Both shoulders sit at the same distance and the same height, and the photograph flattens.


Turn your body about thirty degrees away from the lens, then bring your face back toward it. One shoulder is now nearer than the other, which creates depth, and your jawline gets an angle to sit against. This single change improves more headshots than lighting does.


Then drop the shoulder nearest the camera very slightly, because level shoulders read as tension.


## The chin rule that fixes most bad headshots


‍


Tucking your chin is the universal instinct in front of a camera and the most damaging thing you can do. It compresses the space under your jaw, shortens your neck and puts your forehead closer to the lens than your eyes.


Do the opposite. Push your chin slightly forward, away from your neck, then bring it down a fraction. Forward, then down. It feels unnatural and looks correct, which is true of most posing.


Two related fixes. Lengthen the back of your neck as if the top of your head is being pulled upward, which stops the head sinking into the shoulders. And keep the camera at or just above eye level, since a lens below eye level works against everything above it.


## Standing and seated options


*Shoulders off-square, chin forward, arms free. All three adjustments in one frame.*


‍


Once your shoulders are turned, the standing frame covers most professional use. Weight on the back foot, front knee soft, hands loose.


Arms crossed gets a bad reputation it half deserves: high and tight reads defensive, low and loose with the shoulders back reads settled. Hands in pockets with the thumbs left out works for the same reason it works everywhere: it gives the hands a destination and opens a gap between arm and torso.


Sitting solves the arm problem outright because your forearms get somewhere to rest. The forward lean is the frame that produces engagement: forearms on a desk or knees, leaning in a few inches toward the lens. Leaning in reads as interest, leaning back reads as evaluation.


Wherever hands land, keep them soft and slightly curled rather than flat and splayed, and give them contact with something. Hold nothing legible, since a phone or a coffee cup pulls the eye off your face.


## Expression, and why "smile" is bad direction


*Ask for a reaction, not a smile. The eyes give away which one you got.*


Being told to smile produces a held smile, which is a different shape from a real one and reads as such.


The mechanic worth learning is the slight squint. Real smiles narrow the muscles around the eyes a little, and a mouth-only smile does not, which is why some headshots feel hollow without anyone being able to say why. Tighten very slightly around the eyes and the expression lands.


Get range while you are there: one warm and open, one neutral and direct, one closed-mouth and serious.


## Different headshots for different jobs


For LinkedIn and company directories, crop tight, keep the background quiet and look straight down the lens. Our notes on[choosing the right LinkedIn profile picture](https://www.snappr.com/blog/6-tips-in-choosing-the-right-profile-picture-for-your-linkedin) cover the platform specifics, and[why a headshot is a core piece of personal branding](https://www.snappr.com/blog/your-headshot-a-key-component-of-your-personal-branding) makes the case for treating it as more than an admin task.


If most of your face time happens on video calls, the same chin and camera-height mechanics apply, which we cover in[how to look better in video calls](https://www.snappr.com/blog/how-to-look-ten-times-better-in-video-calls-from-your-home-office) .

## Frequently asked questions


### What is the best pose for a professional headshot?


Turn your body about thirty degrees away from the camera, bring your face back toward the lens, and push your chin slightly forward then down. Keep the shoulder nearest the camera a fraction lower than the other.


### Should I cross my arms in a headshot?


Only if it is loose. Crossed high and tight across the chest reads defensive, while crossed low with relaxed hands and open shoulders reads settled. If warmth matters more than authority in your field, use hands in pockets or a seated pose instead.


### How do I avoid a double chin in a headshot?


Push your chin forward away from your neck, then bring it down slightly. Also lengthen the back of your neck as if the top of your head is being lifted, and keep the camera at or just above eye level rather than below it.


### How many headshot poses do I need?


Three body positions and three expressions is plenty: one standing turned frame, one lean, one seated forward lean, each shot warm, neutral and serious. That covers LinkedIn, a company directory, a conference bio and a press request.
